description: We are USACH Space Program, a student-led aerospace initiative at the University of Santiago de Chile, founded in 2026. We are more than 16 students from different engineering fields, and we learn by doing. We are driven by curiosity and by documenting everything openly. We are looking for people who want to learn with us in data analysis, programming, AI/ML, remote sensing, UX, or science communication.
summary: Zenith is an interactive 3D lunar digital twin that helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in real time.Combining JPL DE440 ephemerides and LOLA topography, Zenith scores site viability across three core metrics: Solar Illumination (E), Earth Visibility (C), and Terrain Slope & Roughness (T). Users can test hardware presets (Crewed HLS, CLPS Lander, or Rover), compare up to four sites side-by-side, and find optimal 30-day landing windows. Featuring dual Simple and Technical modes, shareable scenario links, and Horizons-validated physics, Zenith turns complex Artemis and CLPS trade-offs into instantaneous visual decisions.
details:
Zenith is an interactive 3D lunar digital twin and web app that helps evaluate and compare landing sites and mission dates, with a focus on the harsh conditions of the Lunar South Pole. For any lunar coordinate, whether from our curated Artemis/CLPS catalog or a custom point, it looks at three things: how much sunlight the site gets (Sun elevation plus the local terrain horizon, so we can tell whether it has solar power or sits in dangerous shadow), whether it has a direct line of sight to Earth for continuous radio communication, and how safe the terrain is for landing. For terrain, Zenith uses curated LRO/Artemis data when available, otherwise samples the LOLA South Pole elevation model (120 m/pixel) by fitting a plane to a 3x3 pixel window to get slope and roughness, and as a last resort uses a deterministic estimate. These three results are combined into a single viability score using a weighted average with adjustable weights, and a strict safety rule sits on top: a site is only marked as viable if it has sunlight, Earth visibility and a slope below the spacecraft's limit, no matter how high its score is. Users move through three stages (intro, explore and compare), where they can apply hardware presets (crewed HLS at 5 degrees, a CLPS robotic lander at 10 degrees, a rover at 20 degrees), compare up to four sites side by side, inspect 360-degree horizon profiles and automatically scan for the best 30-day landing windows.

The value of this becomes clear in real missions like Artemis and CLPS, where a delay of just a few days can drastically change polar lighting and Earth visibility. Zenith lets mission planners recalculate the viability of a site instantly and find alternative 30-day windows, which makes re-targeting a mission much faster. The tool also works for two audiences at once: in Technical mode, mission architects get raw data, adjustable weights, horizon masks and CSV export, while in Simple mode students, educators and the public get plain-language explanations of why a site works or fails on a given date. Every choice (date, sites, custom coordinates and lander preset) is also saved in the URL, so a team can share an exact scenario with a single link and everyone sees the same analysis.

To build it, we used Python 3.10+ and FastAPI for the backend and physics engine, following an MVC architecture where the domain logic is pure Python with no web dependencies. The frontend uses native ES Modules (HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript) with Three.js to render the Moon in 3D using 8K NASA SVS textures and topographic relief, without heavy frameworks or Node.js. For data, we rely on JPL DE440 ephemerides, lunar orientation models and NASA LRO LOLA digital elevation models with 120 m/pixel polar coverage. Everything is tested with a Pytest suite that checks our astronomy and ephemeris calculations against JPL Horizons reference cases, and the whole workflow runs through a single script (./run.sh).

What makes Zenith creative is how we approached the constraints around it. Scientific tools often fail in field or restricted environments because of complex builds or cloud dependencies, so we designed Zenith to be offline-first and free of Node.js: the frontend is served directly by FastAPI and ./run.sh automates the data download, which means the app runs fully offline once the ~60 MB dataset is on the machine. We also wanted landing safety to reflect the real limits of each vehicle instead of being a generic number, since a site with excellent sunlight should not be recommended if its 12-degree slope would tip over a crewed lander. Finally, we designed the experience around progressive disclosure: it starts with a clean 3D globe, moves to the sky and horizon of a single site, and ends in a four-site comparison matrix, with the whole interface available in both Spanish and English.
dataRefs: NASA SPICE kernels (NAIF/JPL): DE440s, orientación lunar
JPL Horizons API (casos de referencia para validar efemérides)
LRO LOLA: DEM polar sur LDEM_75S_120M (USGS Astrogeology)
LROC: coordenadas de sitios y productos de iluminación
NASA SVS: texturas LROC color y LDEM del globo
NASA NTRS: Artemis Lunar Surface Data Book, selección de sitios
NASA NSSDC: hojas de datos de la Luna y la Tierra
projectRefs: PGDA (MIT Imbrium): mapas de iluminación y visibilidad de la Tierra, LOLA
Skyfield (cálculo de efemérides), FastAPI, NumPy, Pillow (dependencias de código abierto)
CNES, JAXA (fuentes de coordenadas de sitios)
Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines (fuentes de misiones comerciales)
